claims.text: Thermal exposure of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA drives localized phase separation and chemical ordering.
Mg segregates and forms intermetallic precipitates at phase boundaries during thermal exposure.
The evolving phase-boundary structure promotes formation of an oxide layer with improved adhesion and altered composition.
The modified oxide layer enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
The modified oxide layer reduces corrosion susceptibility relative to the as-cast state.
The initial material is a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution containing disordered phases and nascent intermetallic phases.
Controlled elevated-temperature aging can promote diffusion and phase separation without reaching complete equilibrium.
Aging changes local chemical order and phase-boundary configurations in multiphase HEAs.
Thermal activation causes Mg to diffuse differently from the other alloy constituents.
Differential Mg diffusion causes localized chemical ordering and phase separation.
Mg-rich intermetallic regions are preferential nucleation sites for protective oxide scales.
Oxides nucleated at Mg-rich intermetallic regions are more adherent and compact.
Thermally aged alloys will have an oxide scale with a different composition, potentially including increased Mg-oxide content.
Thermally aged alloys will exhibit lower high-temperature oxidation rates than as-cast controls.
Thermally aged alloys will exhibit lower electrochemical corrosion rates than as-cast controls.
The hypothesis is restricted to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm3 and aging temperatures that promote but do not complete phase separation.
An aging or oxidation range of approximately 700–1100 °C is suitable for testing the proposed evolution.
